title: Saint Athanasius the Apostolic — Biography
text: Saint Athanasius the Apostolic (c. 296 – 373 AD), 20th Pope of Alexandria · Patriarch of All Africa. Saint Athanasius served as the 20th Pope and Patriarch of Alexandria for 45 years — longer than any other bishop of his era — and spent nearly a third of that tenure in exile for his unyielding defense of Nicene Christianity against Arianism. He is the theological father of the Coptic Orthodox Church and the entire Oriental Orthodox tradition. His exile five times under four Roman emperors gave rise to the Latin phrase Athanasius contra mundum — "Athanasius against the world" — a tribute to his refusal to compromise the faith even when almost the entire episcopate capitulated to Arian pressure. Athanasius attended the Council of Nicaea as a deacon and assistant to Bishop Alexander. He became Pope of Alexandria aged ~30 and spent 17 of his 45 years as Pope in exile under five emperors.

title: Saint Athanasius the Apostolic — Key Teachings
text: Key teachings of Saint Athanasius the Apostolic: The full, uncreated divinity of the Son — "of one essence (homoousios) with the Father" • The Incarnation as the means of human deification (theosis): "God became man so that man might become God" • The Holy Spirit as fully divine, not a lesser being • The apostolic canon of Scripture, including the 27 books of the New Testament (listed definitively in his 39th Festal Letter, 367 AD)

title: Saint Athanasius the Apostolic — Quotation
text: He, indeed, assumed humanity that we might become God. He manifested Himself by means of a body that we might perceive the Mind of the unseen Father. He endured the insolence of men that we might inherit immortality.

title: Saint Athanasius the Apostolic — On the Incarnation (De Incarnatione)
text: On the Incarnation (De Incarnatione) (c. 318 AD) by Saint Athanasius the Apostolic: His greatest work, written before the Arian controversy, arguing that the Incarnation was necessary to reverse Adam's corruption. C.S. Lewis wrote the introduction to a modern translation.

title: Saint Athanasius the Apostolic — Against the Arians (Orationes contra Arianos)
text: Against the Arians (Orationes contra Arianos) (c. 339–358 AD) by Saint Athanasius the Apostolic: Four orations demolishing the Arian position that the Son is a creature. Remains the definitive patristic refutation of Arianism.

title: Saint Athanasius the Apostolic — 39th Festal Letter
text: 39th Festal Letter (367 AD) by Saint Athanasius the Apostolic: The first document in history to list the exact 27 books of the New Testament as canonical, unchanged to this day.

title: Saint Athanasius the Apostolic — Life of Saint Anthony (Vita Antonii)
text: Life of Saint Anthony (Vita Antonii) (c. 360 AD) by Saint Athanasius the Apostolic: The founding biography of Christian monasticism, which sparked the desert movement across the Roman world.

title: Saint Augustine of Hippo — Biography
text: Saint Augustine of Hippo (354 – 430 AD), Bishop of Hippo · Doctor of Grace. Saint Augustine was born in Thagaste (modern Algeria) to a Berber family, making him a North African Father. He studied in Carthage, became a Manichaean, and was converted to Christianity in Milan largely through the prayers of his mother, Monica, and the preaching of Saint Ambrose. As Bishop of Hippo, he wrote voluminously against the Pelagian, Donatist, and Manichaean heresies, and his works on grace, free will, original sin, and the Trinity profoundly shaped all subsequent Western theology. While he is more fully integrated into Roman Catholic and Protestant traditions, the Coptic Church honors him as a significant patristic voice from North Africa. Augustine was born to a Berber mother (Monica) and a Roman father (Patricius) in North Africa — making him ethnically African. His theological influence on Western Christianity (both Catholic and Protestant) is unparalleled.

title: Saint Augustine of Hippo — Key Teachings
text: Key teachings of Saint Augustine of Hippo: Original sin: Adam's fall corrupted human nature and transmitted guilt and concupiscence to all descendants • Prevenient grace: human beings cannot turn toward God without divine grace first enabling the will • The Trinity as co-equal, co-eternal Persons sharing one substance • The Church as a mixed body (corpus permixtum) containing both elect and reprobate until the Last Judgment

title: Saint Augustine of Hippo — Quotation
text: Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.

title: Saint Augustine of Hippo — Confessions (Confessiones)
text: Confessions (Confessiones) (c. 397–400 AD) by Saint Augustine of Hippo: The first autobiography in Western literature — a sustained prayer to God tracing Augustine's spiritual journey from Manichaeism to Christianity. "Our heart is restless until it rests in Thee."

source: The City of God (De Civitate Dei)

metadata.name: Saint Augustine of Hippo
metadata.work_title: The City of God (De Civitate Dei)

title: Saint Augustine of Hippo — The City of God (De Civitate Dei)
text: The City of God (De Civitate Dei) (413–426 AD) by Saint Augustine of Hippo: Written after the sack of Rome by Alaric (410), this work distinguishes the City of God from the City of Man and surveys all of human history through a Christian lens.

title: Saint Augustine of Hippo — On the Trinity (De Trinitate)
text: On the Trinity (De Trinitate) (399–422 AD) by Saint Augustine of Hippo: His most technically sophisticated theological work, developing the Western psychological analogy of the Trinity (memory, understanding, will) and defending the Filioque.

title: Saint Augustine of Hippo — Against Pelagius
text: Against Pelagius (412–430 AD) by Saint Augustine of Hippo: A series of writings defending the necessity of divine grace against Pelagius's teaching that human will is sufficient for salvation without grace.

title: Saint Basil the Great — Biography
text: Saint Basil the Great (c. 330 – 379 AD), Archbishop of Caesarea · Cappadocian Father. Saint Basil was Archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia (modern Turkey) and is reckoned one of the Three Holy Hierarchs of Eastern Christianity alongside Gregory the Theologian and John Chrysostom. He organized monastic life in the East with his Longer and Shorter Rules — the basis for all Eastern Christian monasticism, including Coptic monasticism. His treatise On the Holy Spirit definitively demonstrated the full divinity of the Third Person against the Pneumatomachi ("Spirit-fighters"). The Divine Liturgy of Saint Basil is used in the Coptic Orthodox Church on the Sundays of Lent, Apostles' Fast, Holy Week, and special feast days. Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Basil's brother Gregory of Nyssa are the "Three Cappadocians" who secured the Nicene faith after Athanasius. Basil also built the Basileiad — a vast complex of hospitals, hostels, and workshops for the poor — the first such institution in the Christian world.

title: Saint Basil the Great — Key Teachings
text: Key teachings of Saint Basil the Great: The Holy Spirit is co-equal and co-essential with the Father and the Son ("of the same rank and honor") • The Spirit is not named separately in the baptismal formula to preserve the mystery, not to diminish His Godhead • Cenobitic monastic life under a rule as the highest form of Christian discipleship • The theology of the liturgical epiclesis — the Spirit's role in the Eucharistic consecration

title: Saint Basil the Great — Quotation
text: The Spirit is not ranked among created things, but is reckoned with the Father and the Son, and is confessed as God by those who hold right opinions.

source: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)

metadata.name: Saint Basil the Great
metadata.work_title: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)

title: Saint Basil the Great — On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
text: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto) (375 AD) by Saint Basil the Great: The definitive patristic argument for the full divinity of the Holy Spirit, written against the Pneumatomachi ("Spirit-fighters"). Used the liturgical doxology "Glory to the Father, with the Son, together with the Holy Spirit" as evidence.

title: Saint Basil the Great — The Longer and Shorter Rules (Ascetica)
text: The Longer and Shorter Rules (Ascetica) (c. 360–370 AD) by Saint Basil the Great: His monastic rule, still foundational for all Eastern monasticism. Unlike Anthony's hermit ideal, Basil championed communal monastic life serving the poor.

title: Saint Basil the Great — Divine Liturgy of Saint Basil
text: Divine Liturgy of Saint Basil (c. 370 AD) by Saint Basil the Great: Still used in the Coptic Orthodox Church on the Sundays of Lent, Holy Week, Apostles' Fast, and major feasts — a living patristic text in Coptic worship today.

title: Saint Basil the Great — Hexaemeron (Six Days of Creation)
text: Hexaemeron (Six Days of Creation) (c. 370 AD) by Saint Basil the Great: Nine homilies on the six days of creation, remarkable for their engagement with contemporary natural science and their lyrical theological prose.

title: Saint Clement of Alexandria — Biography
text: Saint Clement of Alexandria (c. 150 – c. 215 AD), Head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria. Saint Clement of Alexandria was the second identifiable head of the famous Catechetical School (Didascalion) of Alexandria, predecessor to the great Origen. A convert to Christianity, he traveled widely before settling in Alexandria under the tutelage of Pantaenus, the school's founder. Clement sought to demonstrate that Greek philosophy — especially Plato — was a preparatory schoolmaster (paidagogos) leading the Gentile world to Christ, just as the Law prepared Israel. His major trilogy — Protrepticus (Exhortation), Paedagogus (The Instructor), and Stromata (Miscellanies) — shaped the Alexandrian tradition of deep, intellectually rigorous theology that has characterized the Coptic Church throughout its history. Clement succeeded Pantaenus as head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria and was succeeded by Origen. He pioneered the integration of Greek philosophical learning into Christian theology — a distinctly Alexandrian project.

title: Saint Clement of Alexandria — Key Teachings
text: Key teachings of Saint Clement of Alexandria: Greek philosophy as a partial, preparatory revelation leading toward the fullness of Christ • The "True Gnostic" — the mature Christian who combines faith with deep knowledge (gnosis) of God • The Logos as the eternal Teacher who has always guided humanity toward truth • Allegorical interpretation of Scripture as revealing deeper spiritual realities beyond the literal text

title: Saint Clement of Alexandria — Quotation
text: The Word of God became man so that you might learn from a man how to become God.

title: Saint Clement of Alexandria — Protrepticus (Exhortation to the Greeks)
text: Protrepticus (Exhortation to the Greeks) (c. 190 AD) by Saint Clement of Alexandria: A missionary address to educated pagans arguing that Christianity is the fulfillment of all that Greek philosophy sought. Demonstrates the Alexandrian method of engaging culture with the Gospel.

title: Saint Clement of Alexandria — Paidagogos (The Tutor)
text: Paidagogos (The Tutor) (c. 190–200 AD) by Saint Clement of Alexandria: A guide to Christian ethics in daily life — dress, food, laughter, wealth — showing how Christ the Logos educates the soul.

title: Saint Clement of Alexandria — Stromateis (Miscellanies)
text: Stromateis (Miscellanies) (c. 200 AD) by Saint Clement of Alexandria: Seven volumes of theological notes on the relationship between faith and knowledge, the true Gnostic (Christian sage), and the use of Greek philosophy in Christian thought.

title: Saint Clement of Rome — Biography
text: Saint Clement of Rome (c. 35 – c. 99 AD), Third Bishop of Rome · Apostolic Father. Saint Clement of Rome is considered the third or fourth Bishop of Rome after Peter. He is mentioned by Paul in Philippians 4:3 as a co-worker "whose names are in the Book of Life." His First Epistle to the Corinthians (c. 96 AD), written to resolve a schism in Corinth, is the earliest extant Christian document outside the New Testament and is the oldest example of a bishop exercising pastoral oversight over a distant church. Clement writes with remarkable authority, invoking apostolic tradition and the order of creation to urge the Corinthians toward unity. He suffered martyrdom under the Emperor Trajan. 1 Clement was so highly regarded in the early Church that some manuscripts include it in the New Testament canon. Clement was the fourth bishop of Rome (after Peter, Linus, and Anacletus) and is believed to have known both Peter and Paul personally.

title: Saint Clement of Rome — Key Teachings
text: Key teachings of Saint Clement of Rome: Apostolic order and succession: the Apostles appointed bishops and deacons, who in turn appointed their successors • Hierarchical Church order as willed by God, mirroring the order of creation • Repentance and humility as the foundations of Christian life • The Eucharist as the central act of Christian worship, presided over by the bishop

title: Saint Clement of Rome — Quotation
text: Let each of you be subject to his neighbor, according to the special gift bestowed upon him. Let the strong not despise the weak, and let the weak show respect unto the strong. Let the rich man provide for the wants of the poor; and let the poor man bless God, because He hath given him one by whom his need may be supplied.

source: First Epistle to the Corinthians (1 Clement)

metadata.name: Saint Clement of Rome
metadata.work_title: First Epistle to the Corinthians (1 Clement)

title: Saint Clement of Rome — First Epistle to the Corinthians (1 Clement)
text: First Epistle to the Corinthians (1 Clement) (c. 96 AD) by Saint Clement of Rome: Written to resolve a schism in the Corinthian church, this letter is one of the earliest Christian documents outside the New Testament. It asserts apostolic authority, the importance of church order, and gives one of the earliest descriptions of the Eucharist.

title: Saint Cyprian of Carthage — Biography
text: Saint Cyprian of Carthage (c. 200 – 258 AD), Bishop of Carthage · Martyr. Saint Cyprian was a North African lawyer and rhetorician who converted to Christianity around 246 AD, was elected Bishop of Carthage just two years later, and was martyred under Emperor Valerian in 258. His episcopate was dominated by two crises: the Decian persecution (249–251) and the controversy over rebaptism. His treatise On the Unity of the Church, written during the Novatian schism, articulated with unprecedented clarity the essential connection between visible Church unity, episcopal succession, and salvation. His Letters provide an invaluable picture of mid-third-century African Christianity and its deep interconnection with Alexandria. Cyprian converted to Christianity in his 40s from a wealthy pagan background and became Bishop of Carthage within two years. He was martyred by beheading under Valerian in 258 AD — the first African bishop to die by the sword.

title: Saint Cyprian of Carthage — Key Teachings
text: Key teachings of Saint Cyprian of Carthage: "Outside the Church there is no salvation" (Extra ecclesiam nulla salus) • The bishop as the center of Church unity — the Church is the people united with their bishop • The primacy of Rome is a primacy of honor, not of universal jurisdiction • The necessity of penance and reconciliation for those who lapsed during persecution

source: On the Unity of the Church, §6
title: Saint Cyprian of Carthage — Quotation
text: He can no longer have God for his Father, who has not the Church for his mother... he who gathers elsewhere than in the Church scatters the Church of Christ.

source: On the Unity of the Church (De Catholicae Ecclesiae Unitate)

metadata.name: Saint Cyprian of Carthage
metadata.work_title: On the Unity of the Church (De Catholicae Ecclesiae Unitate)

title: Saint Cyprian of Carthage — On the Unity of the Church (De Catholicae Ecclesiae Unitate)
text: On the Unity of the Church (De Catholicae Ecclesiae Unitate) (251 AD) by Saint Cyprian of Carthage: Written during the Novatian schism, this foundational work articulates the theology of episcopal unity and episcopal succession. Contains the famous phrase: "He cannot have God for his Father who has not the Church for his Mother."

title: Saint Cyprian of Carthage — On the Lapsed (De Lapsis)
text: On the Lapsed (De Lapsis) (251 AD) by Saint Cyprian of Carthage: Addresses how to receive back into communion those Christians who had apostatized under Decian persecution — a major pastoral and theological controversy.

source: On the Lord's Prayer (De Dominica Oratione)

metadata.name: Saint Cyprian of Carthage
metadata.work_title: On the Lord's Prayer (De Dominica Oratione)

title: Saint Cyprian of Carthage — On the Lord's Prayer (De Dominica Oratione)
text: On the Lord's Prayer (De Dominica Oratione) (252 AD) by Saint Cyprian of Carthage: A rich theological commentary on the Our Father, exploring each petition in depth. Remains one of the finest patristic commentaries on the Lord's Prayer.

title: Saint Cyril of Alexandria — Biography
text: Saint Cyril of Alexandria (c. 376 – 444 AD), 24th Pope of Alexandria · Doctor of the Incarnation. Saint Cyril of Alexandria was the 24th Pope and Patriarch of Alexandria and the greatest Christological theologian of the patristic era. His defining achievement was his defeat of Nestorianism at the Council of Ephesus (431 AD), where he secured the title Theotokos (God-Bearer) for the Virgin Mary — a title that encapsulated his theology that Christ is one Person, not two. Against Nestorius, who taught that Mary bore only the human Christ and that the divine and human natures were loosely conjoined, Cyril insisted on the "hypostatic union" (μία φύσις, mia physis) — one nature of the Incarnate Logos — the formula that defines Coptic Christology to this day. His Twelve Anathemas against Nestorius and his commentaries on John's Gospel are pillars of Coptic theology. Cyril's victory at Ephesus (431) secured the title Theotokos for the Virgin Mary and repudiated Nestorius's two-nature Christology. The Coptic Church considers him the theological summit of the Alexandrian tradition.

title: Saint Cyril of Alexandria — Key Teachings
text: Key teachings of Saint Cyril of Alexandria: Mia physis (one nature): "One nature of the incarnate Word of God" — the complete union of divinity and humanity in Christ • Theotokos: Mary is rightly called "Mother of God" because she bore the one Person who is both God and man • The Eucharist as the true Body and Blood of Christ, the Life-giving Flesh that deifies the communicant • The Holy Spirit as the Spirit of the Son, proceeding from the Father through the Son

title: Saint Cyril of Alexandria — Quotation
text: We confess one Christ, one Lord, one Son. And since He is one, we do not divide the Sonship or assign a glory and an honor to the flesh separately... but we confess one Lord Jesus Christ.

title: Saint Cyril of Alexandria — Twelve Anathemas against Nestorius
text: Twelve Anathemas against Nestorius (430 AD) by Saint Cyril of Alexandria: Twelve propositions condemning Nestorian Christology and asserting that Mary is truly Theotokos (God-bearer). The anathemas became the theological standard for the Council of Ephesus.

source: Commentary on the Gospel of John

metadata.name: Saint Cyril of Alexandria
metadata.work_title: Commentary on the Gospel of John

title: Saint Cyril of Alexandria — Commentary on the Gospel of John
text: Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 425–428 AD) by Saint Cyril of Alexandria: His masterpiece of exegesis, treating John's Gospel as the fullest revelation of the Incarnation. Still read as a theological reference today.

title: Saint Cyril of Alexandria — On the Unity of Christ
text: On the Unity of Christ (c. 437 AD) by Saint Cyril of Alexandria: A dialogue arguing for the single subject ("one nature") of the Incarnate Word — the position that defines Oriental Orthodox Christology to this day.

title: Saint Cyril of Alexandria — Paschal Letters
text: Paschal Letters (414–442 AD) by Saint Cyril of Alexandria: Annual letters to the Alexandrian Church announcing the date of Pascha, containing rich theological reflections. 29 survive.

title: Saint Cyril of Jerusalem — Biography
text: Saint Cyril of Jerusalem (c. 313 – 386 AD), Archbishop of Jerusalem · Doctor of the Church. Saint Cyril served as Archbishop of Jerusalem during one of the most turbulent periods of early Christianity, navigating the theological conflicts of the Arian controversy while exiled three times from his see. His enduring legacy is his Catechetical Lectures — 24 homilies addressed to baptismal candidates (catechumens) and the newly baptized. These lectures are the finest surviving example of early Christian mystagogy (explanation of the sacramental mysteries) and are invaluable for understanding how the early Church understood and administered Baptism, Chrismation, the Eucharist, and the Liturgy. They remain a primary reference for Coptic sacramental theology. Cyril was exiled three times for his opposition to Arianism. His Catechetical Lectures are invaluable for their detailed descriptions of 4th-century baptismal, eucharistic, and confirmation rites.

title: Saint Cyril of Jerusalem — Key Teachings
text: Key teachings of Saint Cyril of Jerusalem: Baptism as genuine death and resurrection with Christ — not a symbol but a real spiritual transformation • Chrismation as the gift of the Holy Spirit, the "anointing of the Holy One" received immediately after Baptism • The Eucharist as the true Body and Blood of Christ — "Do not think of the bread and wine as mere bread and wine" • The Church's liturgy as participation in the heavenly liturgy, where Christ is the eternal High Priest

title: Saint Cyril of Jerusalem — Quotation
text: Do not think of the bread and wine as mere bread and wine, for they are the Body and Blood of Christ as the Master Himself has declared. Though your senses suggest otherwise, let faith reassure you.

title: Saint Cyril of Jerusalem — Catechetical Lectures (Catecheses)
text: Catechetical Lectures (Catecheses) (c. 350 AD) by Saint Cyril of Jerusalem: 24 lectures delivered to baptismal candidates in Jerusalem: 18 pre-baptismal and 5 mystagogical (explaining the sacraments to the newly baptized). The most complete catechetical document of the ancient Church.

title: Saint Ephrem the Syrian — Biography
text: Saint Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306 – 373 AD), Deacon of Edessa · Hymn-Writer · Doctor of the Church. Saint Ephrem the Syrian was born in Nisibis (modern Turkey/Syria) and served as a deacon in Edessa until his death. Unlike most Church Fathers who wrote in Greek or Latin, he composed almost entirely in Syriac, making him the greatest theologian of the Syriac tradition. His prolific output of hymns (madrāšê), metrical homilies (memrê), and prose commentaries earned him the title "the Harp of the Holy Spirit." The Syriac Church and its theology — deeply connected to the Coptic Church through shared Oriental Orthodox tradition — is shaped by Ephrem's profound scriptural mysticism. His hymns on the Nativity, Epiphany, the Church, Paradise, and the Resurrection are sung to this day. Called the "Harp of the Holy Spirit," Ephrem wrote almost entirely in poetry. He is the only Syrian Father honored as a Doctor of the Church by Rome and is venerated as a saint in the Coptic tradition. He pioneered using hymns to teach theology to laypeople.

title: Saint Ephrem the Syrian — Key Teachings
text: Key teachings of Saint Ephrem the Syrian: The mystery (rāzā) of the Incarnation: divinity hidden within humanity like fire within iron • Mary as the New Eve who reversed the sin of the first Eve by her obedience • The Eucharist as the "Medicine of Life" — the coals of the divine fire placed on the lips of the faithful • Paradoxical theology: God is known through what He is not; the categories of human knowledge cannot contain Him

title: Saint Ephrem the Syrian — Quotation
text: Lord, do not rebuke me in Your anger or chasten me in Your wrath. Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak. Heal me, O Lord, for my bones are troubled. My soul also is very troubled; but You, O Lord — how long?

title: Saint Ephrem the Syrian — Hymns on the Nativity
text: Hymns on the Nativity (c. 360–373 AD) by Saint Ephrem the Syrian: 28 hymns on the birth of Christ — rich with typology, paradox, and vivid imagery. One of the supreme works of Christian poetry: "The Lord entered into her and became a servant; the Word entered into her and became silent within her."

title: Saint Ephrem the Syrian — Hymns against Heresies
text: Hymns against Heresies (c. 360–373 AD) by Saint Ephrem the Syrian: A series of hymns refuting Gnosticism, Manichaeism, and Arianism, written in poetic meter so that orthodox Christians would sing them and remember the faith.

title: Saint Ephrem the Syrian — Commentary on the Diatessaron
text: Commentary on the Diatessaron (c. 360–373 AD) by Saint Ephrem the Syrian: A commentary on Tatian's Gospel harmony, our most important source for early Syriac Gospel interpretation.

title: Saint Gregory Nazianzus — Biography
text: Saint Gregory Nazianzus (c. 329 – 390 AD), Archbishop of Constantinople · Cappadocian Father. Saint Gregory Nazianzus is one of only three Christians in history called "The Theologian" by the Church, alongside Saint John the Evangelist and Saint Symeon the New Theologian. He served briefly as Archbishop of Constantinople, where he presided over the First Council of Constantinople (381 AD), which extended the Nicene Creed to include the full divinity of the Holy Spirit. His Five Theological Orations, delivered in Constantinople against the Eunomian Arians, are masterpieces of theological precision and rhetorical power, and remain the definitive patristic statement of Trinitarian theology. He resigned from his see rather than cause further division in the Church. Only two figures in Orthodox tradition are called "the Theologian" — St. John the Evangelist and Gregory of Nazianzus. He presided briefly over the First Council of Constantinople (381) before resigning, unable to bear the conflict. He spent his last years writing poetry on his estate.

title: Saint Gregory Nazianzus — Key Teachings
text: Key teachings of Saint Gregory Nazianzus: The Three Persons of the Trinity are distinguished by relations of origin only, not by nature or divinity • The Holy Spirit is fully God: "Is the Spirit God? Most certainly. Is He consubstantial? Yes, if He is God." • Theological language requires apophatic humility — we know more surely what God is not than what He is • The full humanity of Christ as essential to salvation: "What is not assumed is not healed"

title: Saint Gregory Nazianzus — Quotation
text: What is not assumed is not healed; but that which is united to His Godhead is also saved. If only half of Adam fell, then that which Christ assumes and saves may be half also; but if the whole of his nature fell, it must be united to the whole nature of Him that was begotten, and so be saved as a whole.

title: Saint Gregory Nazianzus — Five Theological Orations
text: Five Theological Orations (380 AD) by Saint Gregory Nazianzus: Delivered in Constantinople, these five sermons are the summit of patristic Trinitarian theology — a precise and passionate defense of the full divinity of the Son and the Holy Spirit. They earned him the title "The Theologian."

title: Saint Gregory Nazianzus — Autobiographical Poems
text: Autobiographical Poems (c. 382–390 AD) by Saint Gregory Nazianzus: Remarkable personal poetry including De Vita Sua (On His Own Life) — the longest autobiographical poem in Greek antiquity. They reveal an unusually interior and sensitive patristic figure.

title: Saint Gregory of Nyssa — Biography
text: Saint Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335 – c. 395 AD), Bishop of Nyssa · Cappadocian Father. Saint Gregory of Nyssa was the younger brother of Basil the Great and the most philosophically sophisticated of the Cappadocian Fathers. Though less a man of action than Basil or a preacher than Gregory Nazianzus, he was the deepest theological thinker of the three. His Life of Moses introduced the concept of epektasis — the soul's infinite, ever-deepening progress into the darkness of God's incomprehensible glory — which became foundational for all Eastern Christian mystical theology. His treatises On the Soul and the Resurrection, Against Eunomius, and The Catechetical Oration are among the finest theological works of antiquity. He also contributed decisively to the Council of Constantinople (381 AD). Gregory of Nyssa is the most philosophically sophisticated of the Cappadocians. His concept of epektasis — that the soul eternally grows into God because God is infinite — influenced Christian mysticism across all traditions. He is the only Cappadocian Father who addressed the status of women in theology, drawing on his sister Macrina as a model.

title: Saint Gregory of Nyssa — Key Teachings
text: Key teachings of Saint Gregory of Nyssa: Epektasis: the soul's eternal, ever-deepening progress into God — salvation is not a destination but an eternal journey • The Divine nature is absolutely infinite and incomprehensible — the human mind can never exhaustively know God • The Resurrection will be universal in its scope, restoring all of creation to its original beauty • The image of God in man (imago Dei) as the capacity for virtue, freedom, and participation in the divine nature

title: Saint Gregory of Nyssa — Quotation
text: This is true perfection: not to avoid a wicked life because we fear punishment like slaves; but to do good because we love goodness itself, to love God because He is worthy of love.

title: Saint Gregory of Nyssa — Life of Moses (De Vita Moysis)
text: Life of Moses (De Vita Moysis) (c. 390 AD) by Saint Gregory of Nyssa: A masterpiece of Christian mysticism reading Moses's ascent of Sinai as the paradigm of the soul's infinite ascent into God. Introduces the concept of epektasis — perpetual spiritual progress into inexhaustible divine infinity.

source: On the Soul and the Resurrection (De Anima et Resurrectione)
